tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.content:
1	# Spec v1: frozen specification
2	
3	Status: FROZEN. No `TODO(decision)` markers remain.
4	
5	Phase 2 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 2 requirements](phase2-requirements.md) govern token implementation where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, AccessControl delegates compliance administration, revoking eligibility preserves existing balances, and pause/freeze/forced transfer are not implemented in this phase. See [implementation decisions](../phase2-implementation.md) for the exact API and scope. The original requirements below remain preserved for audit comparison.
6	
7	Phase 3 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 3 requirements](phase3-requirements.md) govern AssetFactory and AssetSale where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, the function names change (`authorizeIssuer`, `revokeIssuer`, `buyTokens`, `pricePerToken`), the registry gains `getAsset` / `getAssetCount` with description and asset-type metadata, and a sale can be closed so unsold inventory can be recovered. The decisions are recorded in that file. The reentrancy requirement and invariant 8 below still apply.
8	
9	How this version was produced: human decisions, with AI-assisted research. The research sessions are logged in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Changes from `spec-v0.md` are explained in section 10.
10	
11	## 1. Problem and trust model
12	
13	**Problem**: real-world asset ownership is opaque, settlement is slow, and compliance tracking is manual. Traditional fund administration relies on intermediaries for record-keeping, transfer approval, and settlement, introducing delay and counterparty risk.
14	
15	**Why a blockchain**: an Ethereum smart contract provides an immutable, publicly auditable share register. Transfer rules (whitelist, freeze, pause) are enforced in code rather than by a custodian. Settlement is atomic — a buyer pays ETH and receives tokens in a single transaction, eliminating counterparty risk. No intermediary can alter the ownership record.
16	
17	**Trust model**: the issuer is trusted to correctly describe the off-chain asset and to maintain the legal register that backs the tokens. The on-chain token is a share register only — the legal claim (e.g. beneficial interest in the fund) sits off-chain in a subscription agreement. The platform admin is trusted to authorise only legitimate issuers.
18	
19	**Out of trust scope**: oracle price accuracy, issuer solvency, off-chain legal enforceability.
20	
21	## 2. Asset and scope
22	
23	Instrument: **fictional real estate investment fund** — Campus Property Fund.
24	
25	| Field | Value |
26	|---|---|
27	| Token name | Campus Property Token |
28	| Symbol | CPT |
29	| Total supply | 10 000 CPT |
30	| Token decimals | 0 (whole units) |
31	| Initial sale price | 0.001 testnet ETH / token |
32	| Issuer | MetaMask Wallet A |
33	| Investor 1 | MetaMask Wallet B |
34	| Investor 2 | MetaMask Wallet C |
35	
36	A second demo asset, Digital Licensing Revenue Pool (symbol: DLP), will be deployed using the same contracts with different metadata to demonstrate the multi-asset registry.
37	
38	Both assets are ERC-20 tokens representing fractional interests in a fictional fund. Tokenising unique NFTs or enforcing actual intellectual-property rights is out of scope.
39	
40	## 3. Roles
41	
42	| Actor | Can | Cannot |
43	|---|---|---|
44	| Platform admin | authorise issuer wallets; deauthorise issuer wallets | hold tokens; buy assets |
45	| Authorised issuer | create assets (sets token name, symbol, supply, sale price at creation); whitelist investor addresses; allocate tokens to the sale contract; withdraw ETH proceeds from the sale contract; freeze an individual investor address; unfreeze; pause all transfers; unpause | control another issuer's asset; change the sale price after creation |
46	| Investor | connect wallet; buy tokens from the sale contract (if whitelisted); transfer tokens to another whitelisted address; view own balance | buy if not whitelisted; transfer to non-whitelisted address |
47	
48	An issuer cannot modify the whitelist, freeze state, or pause state of a token they did not deploy.
49	
50	## 4. Contracts and state
51	
52	### AssetToken.sol
53	
54	Purpose: ERC-20 token with compliance controls.
55	
56	State variables:
57	- `address public issuer` — set at deployment, immutable in practice
58	- `mapping(address => bool) public whitelist` — addresses permitted to hold and transfer tokens
59	- `bool public paused` — when true, all transfers revert
60	- `mapping(address => bool) public frozen` — individual addresses barred from sending or receiving
61	
62	Calls: none external (pure ERC-20 logic + compliance hooks).
63	
64	**Price model**: fixed price set at deployment, stored in AssetSale (not AssetToken). AssetToken has no knowledge of price.
65	
66	**Extra features in scope**: whitelist (required to receive or send), pause (issuer halts all transfers globally), freeze (issuer bars one address), forced transfer (issuer can move tokens out of a frozen address to recover them).
67	
68	**Out of scope for AssetToken**: redemption, yield/dividend, NAV oracle, upgradeability.
69	
70	### AssetFactory.sol
71	
72	Purpose: authorise issuers; deploy and register asset contracts.
73	
74	State variables:
75	- `address public admin` — platform admin, set in constructor
76	- `mapping(address => bool) public authorisedIssuers`
77	- `address[] public assets` — list of all deployed AssetToken addresses
78	- `mapping(address => address) public tokenToSale` — maps each AssetToken to its AssetSale
79	
80	Calls: deploys `AssetToken` and `AssetSale`.
81	
82	### AssetSale.sol
83	
84	Purpose: hold sale inventory; accept fixed-price ETH payments; hold proceeds for issuer withdrawal.
85	
86	State variables:
87	- `AssetToken public token`
88	- `uint256 public priceWei` — fixed price per token in wei, set at deployment
89	- `address public issuer`
90	
91	**DvP design**: escrow. The issuer calls `allocate(amount)`, transferring tokens from their wallet into the AssetSale contract. A buyer calls `buy(amount)` with `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; tokens transfer to the buyer immediately and ETH is held in the contract. The issuer later calls `withdrawProceeds()` to collect ETH.
92	
93	**Subscription flow**: instant. `buy` reverts if the caller is not whitelisted or if the contract holds fewer tokens than requested; otherwise the transfer is immediate with no approval queue.
94	
95	**Reentrancy requirement**: `withdrawProceeds` must use the checks-effects-interactions pattern — zero the internal ETH balance before calling out — or apply a reentrancy guard. An issuer whose address is a contract could otherwise re-enter and drain more ETH than owed.
96	
97	## 5. Functions
98	
99	Every external function, who may call it, preconditions, effects, events emitted, and what must revert.
100	
101	| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
102	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
103	| `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | — | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = true` | `IssuerAuthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr already authorised |
104	| `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | addr is authorised | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = false` | `IssuerDeauthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr not authorised. **Note**: deauthorisation prevents future calls to `createAsset` only. Existing deployed AssetToken and AssetSale contracts continue operating; the admin cannot revoke an issuer's authority over contracts they have already deployed. |
105	| `AssetFactory.createAsset(name, symbol, supply, priceWei)` | authorised issuer | priceWei > 0; supply > 0 | deploys AssetToken, mints supply to issuer; deploys AssetSale; records both in registry | `AssetCreated(token, sale, issuer)` | caller not authorised |
106	| `AssetToken.addToWhitelist(address)` | issuer | — | `whitelist[addr] = true` | `Whitelisted(addr)` | caller != issuer |
107	| `AssetToken.removeFromWhitelist(address)` | issuer | addr has zero balance | `whitelist[addr] = false` | `RemovedFromWhitelist(addr)` | caller != issuer; addr has non-zero balance. **Recovery flow when addr is frozen**: issuer must (1) call `forcedTransfer(addr, safeAddr, balance)` to empty addr's holdings, then (2) call `removeFromWhitelist(addr)`. |
108	| `AssetToken.transfer(to, amount)` | token holder | `whitelist[to]`; `!paused`; `!frozen[from]`; `!frozen[to]` | standard ERC-20 transfer | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` | any precondition false |
109	| `AssetToken.transferFrom(from, to, amount)` | approved spender | same as transfer | same as transfer | `Transfer` | any precondition false |
110	| `AssetToken.pause()` | issuer | `!paused` | `paused = true` | `Paused()` | caller != issuer; already paused |
111	| `AssetToken.unpause()` | issuer | `paused` | `paused = false` | `Unpaused()` | caller != issuer; not paused |
112	| `AssetToken.freeze(address)` | issuer | `!frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = true` | `Frozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; already frozen |
113	| `AssetToken.unfreeze(address)` | issuer | `frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = false` | `Unfrozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; not frozen |
114	| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | issuer | `whitelist[to]`; `!frozen[to]` | transfers regardless of `frozen[from]` and regardless of `paused` — this is the issuer's emergency recovery mechanism | `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller != issuer; `to` not whitelisted; `to` is frozen |
115	| `AssetSale.allocate(uint256 amount)` | issuer | issuer ERC-20 balance >= amount; issuer has approved AssetSale | transfers tokens from issuer to AssetSale | `Allocated(amount)` | caller != issuer; balance insufficient |
116	| `AssetSale.buy(uint256 amount)` | investor | `whitelist[msg.sender]`; `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; AssetSale token balance >= amount | transfers tokens to buyer; ETH held in contract | `Purchased(buyer, amount)` | any precondition false |
117	| `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | ETH balance > 0 | sends full ETH balance to issuer | `ProceedsWithdrawn(amount)` | caller != issuer; no ETH to withdraw |
118	
119	## 6. Invariants
120	
121	Properties that must hold after any sequence of calls. These become invariant and unit tests.
122	
123	1. **Whitelist invariant**: every address with a non-zero CPT balance is on the whitelist. (`balanceOf(addr) > 0 → whitelist[addr] == true`)
124	2. **Supply invariant**: `totalSupply()` equals the sum of all individual balances at all times.
125	3. **Sale proceeds invariant**: ETH held by AssetSale equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus total ETH withdrawn by the issuer.
126	4. **Transfer gate invariant**: no transfer to a non-whitelisted address ever succeeds; every such attempt reverts.
127	5. **Pause invariant**: when `paused == true`, no `transfer` or `transferFrom` succeeds (except `forcedTransfer` by issuer).
128	6. **Freeze invariant**: when `frozen[addr] == true`, `addr` cannot send tokens via `transfer` or `transferFrom`.
129	7. **Issuer isolation invariant**: address X can only call `addToWhitelist`, `pause`, `freeze`, `forcedTransfer`, `allocate`, or `withdrawProceeds` on an AssetToken / AssetSale that X deployed.
130	8. **Reentrancy invariant**: after `withdrawProceeds` completes, the ETH balance tracked by AssetSale is zero, regardless of any re-entrant calls made during the ETH send. Implementation must zero the balance before the external call.
131	
132	## 7. Frontend
133	
134	**Admin dashboard** (`/admin`)
135	- Shows: list of authorised issuers (from `AssetFactory`)
136	- Actions: authorise new issuer (enter address → `authoriseIssuer`); deauthorise (→ `deauthoriseIssuer`)
137	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.authorisedIssuers`, `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer`, `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer`
138	
139	**Issuer dashboard** (`/issuer`)
140	- Shows: list of assets the connected wallet deployed; per-asset: token balance, AssetSale inventory, ETH proceeds
141	- Actions: create new asset (form: name, symbol, supply, price → `createAsset`); allocate tokens (enter amount → approve then `allocate`); whitelist investor (enter address → `addToWhitelist`); withdraw proceeds (→ `withdrawProceeds`)
142	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.createAsset`, `AssetToken.addToWhitelist`, `AssetSale.allocate`, `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds`
143	
144	**Investor dashboard** (`/investor`)
145	- Shows: all assets in factory registry; for each: name, symbol, price, available tokens; own holdings
146	- Actions: buy tokens (enter amount, pay ETH → `buy`); transfer tokens (enter recipient + amount → `transfer`)
147	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.assets`, `AssetSale.buy`, `AssetToken.transfer`
148	
149	Each page connects via MetaMask using ethers.js `BrowserProvider`. Deployed contract addresses are read from a JSON config file generated by the deploy script.
150	
151	## 8. Out of scope
152	
153	- NFT-based unique assets — per-asset complexity out of MVP scope
154	- Redemption / buyback — out of scope
155	- Yield / dividend distribution — out of scope
156	- NAV oracle or price updates after creation — out of scope; price is fixed at deployment
157	- Multi-jurisdiction compliance rules beyond a single whitelist — out of scope
158	- Actual legal enforceability of the on-chain record — out of scope
159	- Governance or on-chain voting — out of scope
160	- Gas optimisation for large investor sets — out of scope for MVP
161	
162	## 9. Assumptions
163	
164	- Network: Sepolia testnet (chain ID 11155111) for integration; Hardhat local network (chain ID 31337) for development
165	- Token decimals: 0 — whole units only, consistent with fractional-unit model where each token represents one equal share
166	- Test wallets: three Hardhat accounts (index 0 = admin, 1 = issuer, 2 = investor) for local tests; three MetaMask burner wallets on Sepolia for demo
167	- Toolchain: Node.js ≥ 18, Hardhat 3.x (installed: 3.21.0), OpenZeppelin Contracts 5.x (installed: 5.6.1), ethers.js 6.x
168	- Frontend: React 18, Vite, ethers.js 6.x
169	- `.env` holds `TESTNET_RPC_URL`, `PRIVATE_KEY`, `ETHERSCAN_API_KEY` — never committed
170	
171	## 10. Changes from v0

# Spec v1: frozen specification

Status: FROZEN. No `TODO(decision)` markers remain.

Phase 2 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 2 requirements](phase2-requirements.md) govern token implementation where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, AccessControl delegates compliance administration, revoking eligibility preserves existing balances, and pause/freeze/forced transfer are not implemented in this phase. See [implementation decisions](../phase2-implementation.md) for the exact API and scope. The original requirements below remain preserved for audit comparison.

Phase 3 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 3 requirements](phase3-requirements.md) govern AssetFactory and AssetSale where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, the function names change (`authorizeIssuer`, `revokeIssuer`, `buyTokens`, `pricePerToken`), the registry gains `getAsset` / `getAssetCount` with description and asset-type metadata, and a sale can be closed so unsold inventory can be recovered. The decisions are recorded in that file. The reentrancy requirement and invariant 8 below still apply.

How this version was produced: human decisions, with AI-assisted research. The research sessions are logged in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Changes from `spec-v0.md` are explained in section 10.

## 1. Problem and trust model

**Problem**: real-world asset ownership is opaque, settlement is slow, and compliance tracking is manual. Traditional fund administration relies on intermediaries for record-keeping, transfer approval, and settlement, introducing delay and counterparty risk.

**Why a blockchain**: an Ethereum smart contract provides an immutable, publicly auditable share register. Transfer rules (whitelist, freeze, pause) are enforced in code rather than by a custodian. Settlement is atomic — a buyer pays ETH and receives tokens in a single transaction, eliminating counterparty risk. No intermediary can alter the ownership record.

**Trust model**: the issuer is trusted to correctly describe the off-chain asset and to maintain the legal register that backs the tokens. The on-chain token is a share register only — the legal claim (e.g. beneficial interest in the fund) sits off-chain in a subscription agreement. The platform admin is trusted to authorise only legitimate issuers.

**Out of trust scope**: oracle price accuracy, issuer solvency, off-chain legal enforceability.

## 2. Asset and scope

Instrument: **fictional real estate investment fund** — Campus Property Fund.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Token name | Campus Property Token |
| Symbol | CPT |
| Total supply | 10 000 CPT |
| Token decimals | 0 (whole units) |
| Initial sale price | 0.001 testnet ETH / token |
| Issuer | MetaMask Wallet A |
| Investor 1 | MetaMask Wallet B |
| Investor 2 | MetaMask Wallet C |

A second demo asset, Digital Licensing Revenue Pool (symbol: DLP), will be deployed using the same contracts with different metadata to demonstrate the multi-asset registry.

Both assets are ERC-20 tokens representing fractional interests in a fictional fund. Tokenising unique NFTs or enforcing actual intellectual-property rights is out of scope.

## 3. Roles

| Actor | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Platform admin | authorise issuer wallets; deauthorise issuer wallets | hold tokens; buy assets |
| Authorised issuer | create assets (sets token name, symbol, supply, sale price at creation); whitelist investor addresses; allocate tokens to the sale contract; withdraw ETH proceeds from the sale contract; freeze an individual investor address; unfreeze; pause all transfers; unpause | control another issuer's asset; change the sale price after creation |
| Investor | connect wallet; buy tokens from the sale contract (if whitelisted); transfer tokens to another whitelisted address; view own balance | buy if not whitelisted; transfer to non-whitelisted address |

An issuer cannot modify the whitelist, freeze state, or pause state of a token they did not deploy.

## 4. Contracts and state

### AssetToken.sol

Purpose: ERC-20 token with compliance controls.

State variables:
- `address public issuer` — set at deployment, immutable in practice
- `mapping(address => bool) public whitelist` — addresses permitted to hold and transfer tokens
- `bool public paused` — when true, all transfers revert
- `mapping(address => bool) public frozen` — individual addresses barred from sending or receiving

Calls: none external (pure ERC-20 logic + compliance hooks).

**Price model**: fixed price set at deployment, stored in AssetSale (not AssetToken). AssetToken has no knowledge of price.

**Extra features in scope**: whitelist (required to receive or send), pause (issuer halts all transfers globally), freeze (issuer bars one address), forced transfer (issuer can move tokens out of a frozen address to recover them).

**Out of scope for AssetToken**: redemption, yield/dividend, NAV oracle, upgradeability.

### AssetFactory.sol

Purpose: authorise issuers; deploy and register asset contracts.

State variables:
- `address public admin` — platform admin, set in constructor
- `mapping(address => bool) public authorisedIssuers`
- `address[] public assets` — list of all deployed AssetToken addresses
- `mapping(address => address) public tokenToSale` — maps each AssetToken to its AssetSale

Calls: deploys `AssetToken` and `AssetSale`.

### AssetSale.sol

Purpose: hold sale inventory; accept fixed-price ETH payments; hold proceeds for issuer withdrawal.

State variables:
- `AssetToken public token`
- `uint256 public priceWei` — fixed price per token in wei, set at deployment
- `address public issuer`

**DvP design**: escrow. The issuer calls `allocate(amount)`, transferring tokens from their wallet into the AssetSale contract. A buyer calls `buy(amount)` with `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; tokens transfer to the buyer immediately and ETH is held in the contract. The issuer later calls `withdrawProceeds()` to collect ETH.

**Subscription flow**: instant. `buy` reverts if the caller is not whitelisted or if the contract holds fewer tokens than requested; otherwise the transfer is immediate with no approval queue.

**Reentrancy requirement**: `withdrawProceeds` must use the checks-effects-interactions pattern — zero the internal ETH balance before calling out — or apply a reentrancy guard. An issuer whose address is a contract could otherwise re-enter and drain more ETH than owed.

## 5. Functions

Every external function, who may call it, preconditions, effects, events emitted, and what must revert.

| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | — | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = true` | `IssuerAuthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr already authorised |
| `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | addr is authorised | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = false` | `IssuerDeauthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr not authorised. **Note**: deauthorisation prevents future calls to `createAsset` only. Existing deployed AssetToken and AssetSale contracts continue operating; the admin cannot revoke an issuer's authority over contracts they have already deployed. |
| `AssetFactory.createAsset(name, symbol, supply, priceWei)` | authorised issuer | priceWei > 0; supply > 0 | deploys AssetToken, mints supply to issuer; deploys AssetSale; records both in registry | `AssetCreated(token, sale, issuer)` | caller not authorised |
| `AssetToken.addToWhitelist(address)` | issuer | — | `whitelist[addr] = true` | `Whitelisted(addr)` | caller != issuer |
| `AssetToken.removeFromWhitelist(address)` | issuer | addr has zero balance | `whitelist[addr] = false` | `RemovedFromWhitelist(addr)` | caller != issuer; addr has non-zero balance. **Recovery flow when addr is frozen**: issuer must (1) call `forcedTransfer(addr, safeAddr, balance)` to empty addr's holdings, then (2) call `removeFromWhitelist(addr)`. |
| `AssetToken.transfer(to, amount)` | token holder | `whitelist[to]`; `!paused`; `!frozen[from]`; `!frozen[to]` | standard ERC-20 transfer | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` | any precondition false |
| `AssetToken.transferFrom(from, to, amount)` | approved spender | same as transfer | same as transfer | `Transfer` | any precondition false |
| `AssetToken.pause()` | issuer | `!paused` | `paused = true` | `Paused()` | caller != issuer; already paused |
| `AssetToken.unpause()` | issuer | `paused` | `paused = false` | `Unpaused()` | caller != issuer; not paused |
| `AssetToken.freeze(address)` | issuer | `!frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = true` | `Frozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; already frozen |
| `AssetToken.unfreeze(address)` | issuer | `frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = false` | `Unfrozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; not frozen |
| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | issuer | `whitelist[to]`; `!frozen[to]` | transfers regardless of `frozen[from]` and regardless of `paused` — this is the issuer's emergency recovery mechanism | `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller != issuer; `to` not whitelisted; `to` is frozen |
| `AssetSale.allocate(uint256 amount)` | issuer | issuer ERC-20 balance >= amount; issuer has approved AssetSale | transfers tokens from issuer to AssetSale | `Allocated(amount)` | caller != issuer; balance insufficient |
| `AssetSale.buy(uint256 amount)` | investor | `whitelist[msg.sender]`; `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; AssetSale token balance >= amount | transfers tokens to buyer; ETH held in contract | `Purchased(buyer, amount)` | any precondition false |
| `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | ETH balance > 0 | sends full ETH balance to issuer | `ProceedsWithdrawn(amount)` | caller != issuer; no ETH to withdraw |

## 6. Invariants

Properties that must hold after any sequence of calls. These become invariant and unit tests.

1. **Whitelist invariant**: every address with a non-zero CPT balance is on the whitelist. (`balanceOf(addr) > 0 → whitelist[addr] == true`)
2. **Supply invariant**: `totalSupply()` equals the sum of all individual balances at all times.
3. **Sale proceeds invariant**: ETH held by AssetSale equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus total ETH withdrawn by the issuer.
4. **Transfer gate invariant**: no transfer to a non-whitelisted address ever succeeds; every such attempt reverts.
5. **Pause invariant**: when `paused == true`, no `transfer` or `transferFrom` succeeds (except `forcedTransfer` by issuer).
6. **Freeze invariant**: when `frozen[addr] == true`, `addr` cannot send tokens via `transfer` or `transferFrom`.
7. **Issuer isolation invariant**: address X can only call `addToWhitelist`, `pause`, `freeze`, `forcedTransfer`, `allocate`, or `withdrawProceeds` on an AssetToken / AssetSale that X deployed.
8. **Reentrancy invariant**: after `withdrawProceeds` completes, the ETH balance tracked by AssetSale is zero, regardless of any re-entrant calls made during the ETH send. Implementation must zero the balance before the external call.

## 7. Frontend

**Admin dashboard** (`/admin`)
- Shows: list of authorised issuers (from `AssetFactory`)
- Actions: authorise new issuer (enter address → `authoriseIssuer`); deauthorise (→ `deauthoriseIssuer`)
- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.authorisedIssuers`, `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer`, `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer`

**Issuer dashboard** (`/issuer`)
- Shows: list of assets the connected wallet deployed; per-asset: token balance, AssetSale inventory, ETH proceeds
- Actions: create new asset (form: name, symbol, supply, price → `createAsset`); allocate tokens (enter amount → approve then `allocate`); whitelist investor (enter address → `addToWhitelist`); withdraw proceeds (→ `withdrawProceeds`)
- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.createAsset`, `AssetToken.addToWhitelist`, `AssetSale.allocate`, `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds`

**Investor dashboard** (`/investor`)
- Shows: all assets in factory registry; for each: name, symbol, price, available tokens; own holdings
- Actions: buy tokens (enter amount, pay ETH → `buy`); transfer tokens (enter recipient + amount → `transfer`)
- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.assets`, `AssetSale.buy`, `AssetToken.transfer`

Each page connects via MetaMask using ethers.js `BrowserProvider`. Deployed contract addresses are read from a JSON config file generated by the deploy script.

## 8. Out of scope

- NFT-based unique assets — per-asset complexity out of MVP scope
- Redemption / buyback — out of scope
- Yield / dividend distribution — out of scope
- NAV oracle or price updates after creation — out of scope; price is fixed at deployment
- Multi-jurisdiction compliance rules beyond a single whitelist — out of scope
- Actual legal enforceability of the on-chain record — out of scope
- Governance or on-chain voting — out of scope
- Gas optimisation for large investor sets — out of scope for MVP

## 9. Assumptions

- Network: Sepolia testnet (chain ID 11155111) for integration; Hardhat local network (chain ID 31337) for development
- Token decimals: 0 — whole units only, consistent with fractional-unit model where each token represents one equal share
- Test wallets: three Hardhat accounts (index 0 = admin, 1 = issuer, 2 = investor) for local tests; three MetaMask burner wallets on Sepolia for demo
- Toolchain: Node.js ≥ 18, Hardhat 3.x (installed: 3.21.0), OpenZeppelin Contracts 5.x (installed: 5.6.1), ethers.js 6.x
- Frontend: React 18, Vite, ethers.js 6.x
- `.env` holds `TESTNET_RPC_URL`, `PRIVATE_KEY`, `ETHERSCAN_API_KEY` — never committed

## 10. Changes from v0

| Change | Why | AI influence |
|---|---|---|
| Narrowed scope to one real-estate fund + one digital asset | Keeps MVP deliverable within project timeline | No |
| Defined three concrete contracts (AssetToken, AssetFactory, AssetSale) | Makes responsibilities and security boundaries explicit | No — human design decision (Phase 1 roadmap) |
| Fixed sale price set at deployment (not issuer-set NAV) | Eliminates price oracle dependency; simplifies MVP | No |
| Instant subscription flow (not request-and-approve) | Reduces contract complexity; investor experience is clearer | No |
| Whitelist + pause + freeze + forced transfer as in-scope features | Directly addresses the "permissioning and compliance" requirement from v0 | No |
| Frontend split into three role-based dashboards | Matches the three-role model; each role sees only relevant actions | No |

1	# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 2: Asset Tokenisation and Compliance
2	
3	## Project Context
4	
5	We are developing a decentralised application (dApp) titled **Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum** for the NTU SC4053 Blockchain Technology Development Project.
6	
7	The application simulates an institutional real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation platform, inspired by financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC.
8	
9	Users will eventually be able to create tokenised assets, purchase tokens using testnet ETH, manage investor permissions, and transfer tokens between eligible wallets.
10	
11	The project is being developed in six sequential phases:
12	
13	1. Project Foundation and Architecture — COMPLETED
14	2. Asset Tokenisation and Compliance — CURRENT PHASE
15	3. Asset Registry and Primary Issuance
16	4. Frontend and MetaMask Integration
17	5. End-to-End Integration and Testnet Deployment
18	6. Security Audit, AI Evaluation and Final Submission
19	
20	**Your task is to fully implement Phase 2, including Solidity development, automated testing, validation, and technical documentation.**
21	
22	Do not implement functionality belonging to later phases.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Step 1: Inspect the Existing Repository
27	
28	Before writing any code:
29	
30	1. Read the existing README, project specifications, architecture documents, and relevant source files.
31	2. Inspect the Hardhat configuration, Solidity compiler version, OpenZeppelin version, package dependencies, and testing framework.
32	3. Understand the architecture established in Phase 1.
33	4. Identify any existing smart contracts or tests relevant to Phase 2.
34	5. Run the existing baseline tests, if available.
35	6. Preserve working Phase 1 code and established project conventions.
36	
37	If there are minor differences between this prompt and the existing repository architecture, adapt the implementation to preserve compatibility. Document any meaningful architectural decisions.
38	
39	Do not unnecessarily reinstall dependencies, overwrite configurations, introduce new frameworks, or restructure the project.
40	
41	## Step 2: Implement `AssetToken.sol`
42	
43	Create or complete:
44	
45	`contracts/AssetToken.sol`
46	
47	This is the core token contract representing fractional interests in a simulated real-world or digital asset.
48	
49	### 2.1 ERC-20 Implementation
50	
51	Use OpenZeppelin's ERC-20 implementation rather than writing token accounting from scratch.
52	
53	The contract must support:
54	
55	- Token name and symbol.
56	- Fixed initial token supply.
57	- Token balances.
58	- Standard `transfer`, `approve`, `allowance`, and `transferFrom` functionality.
59	- ERC-20 `Transfer` and `Approval` events.
60	- Ownership records derived from token balances.
61	
62	The contract constructor should accept:
63	
64	```solidity
65	constructor(
66	    string memory name_,
67	    string memory symbol_,
68	    uint256 initialSupply_,
69	    address issuer_
70	)
71	```
72	
73	Expected behaviour:
74	
75	- The token name and symbol are configured at deployment.
76	- `initialSupply_` is minted to the issuer's wallet.
77	- `totalSupply()` returns the correct fixed supply.
78	- `balanceOf(issuer_)` initially equals `initialSupply_`.
79	- Token decimals are set to **0**, representing whole asset units.
80	- Further minting is not permitted after deployment.
81	- Zero issuer addresses and zero initial supply must be rejected.
82	
83	For example:
84	
85	```text
86	Token Name: Campus Property Token
87	Symbol: CPT
88	Initial Supply: 10,000
89	Decimals: 0
90	
91	Issuer Balance: 10,000 CPT
92	Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
93	```
94	
95	The MVP uses whole token units. Do not automatically multiply the supply by 10^18.
96	
97	### 2.2 Role-Based Access Control
98	
99	Implement role-based permissions using OpenZeppelin AccessControl.
100	
101	At minimum, define:
102	
103	```solidity
104	bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE =
105	    keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE");
106	```
107	
108	The issuer supplied during deployment should initially receive:
109	
110	- `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`
111	- `COMPLIANCE_ROLE`
112	
113	The issuer must also automatically be whitelisted.
114	
115	Only authorised compliance administrators may approve or revoke investor eligibility.
116	
117	Important implementation detail: **Do not assume `msg.sender` is always the issuer during construction.**
118	
119	In Phase 3, the token contract may be deployed by an asset factory on behalf of an issuer. Therefore, roles must be explicitly assigned to the `issuer_` constructor argument rather than blindly assigned to the deploying contract.
120	
121	Do not implement the platform-wide issuer approval system yet; that belongs to Phase 3.
122	
123	### 2.3 Investor Whitelisting
124	
125	Implement an on-chain investor eligibility registry.
126	
127	Suggested state variable:
128	
129	```solidity
130	mapping(address => bool) public isWhitelisted;
131	```
132	
133	Required function:
134	
135	```solidity
136	function setWhitelisted(
137	    address investor,
138	    bool approved
139	) external;
140	```
141	
142	Requirements:
143	
144	1. Only addresses holding `COMPLIANCE_ROLE` may call the function.
145	2. Setting `approved = true` adds an investor to the whitelist.
146	3. Setting `approved = false` revokes an investor's eligibility.
147	4. Zero addresses cannot be whitelisted.
148	5. Emit a `WhitelistUpdated` event when eligibility changes.
149	6. Whitelist status must be publicly readable.
150	
151	An approved investor is permitted to hold and receive the asset tokens.
152	
153	An investor removed from the whitelist must no longer be able to send or receive tokens, even if they still have a positive token balance.
154	
155	Do not forcibly confiscate or burn tokens when whitelist access is revoked.
156	
157	### 2.4 Enforce Transfer Restrictions
158	
159	This is the most important functionality of Phase 2.
160	
161	Modify ERC-20 transfer behaviour so that tokens can only move between whitelisted addresses.
162	
163	Expected behaviour:
164	
165	| Sender | Recipient | Result |
166	|---|---|---|
167	| Whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer succeeds |
168	| Whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
169	| Not whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
170	| Not whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
171	
172	**The restrictions must be enforced inside the token contract itself, not just in a separate purchasing contract or frontend.**
173	
174	Both `transfer()` and `transferFrom()` must respect the restrictions.
175	
176	If OpenZeppelin Contracts v5 is installed, use the appropriate ERC-20 `_update()` override to enforce transfer eligibility. If an older compatible version is already used by the project, implement the equivalent restriction using the supported hook for that version.
177	
178	Do not downgrade OpenZeppelin or use deprecated methods just to follow an example.
179	
180	Handle the zero-address minting case correctly during initial deployment.
181	
182	The initial mint must succeed even though the zero address is not an eligible investor.
183	
184	Avoid adding unnecessary restrictions to standard ERC-20 approval functionality unless required for security.
185	
186	### 2.5 Contract Events and Errors
187	
188	Implement clear events for compliance operations, such as:
189	
190	```solidity
191	event WhitelistUpdated(
192	    address indexed investor,
193	    bool approved,
194	    address indexed operator
195	);
196	```
197	
198	Use descriptive custom errors where appropriate.
199	
200	The code should clearly distinguish failures caused by:
201	
202	- Unauthorised compliance administration.
203	- Invalid wallet addresses.
204	- Non-whitelisted senders.
205	- Non-whitelisted recipients.
206	- Invalid constructor parameters.
207	
208	Keep the implementation concise and readable.
209	
210	### 2.6 Future Compatibility
211	
212	The contract must be designed to support Phase 3 without major redesign.
213	
214	In Phase 3, an `AssetSale` contract will temporarily hold token inventory and distribute tokens to approved investors.
215	
216	Therefore:
217	
218	- Compliance administrators must be able to whitelist smart-contract addresses, not only externally owned wallets.
219	- Whitelisted sale contracts must be capable of receiving and transferring asset tokens.
220	- The token should work when instantiated by a factory contract.
221	- The token must not depend on any frontend implementation.
222	- Each deployed token must maintain independent balances, roles, and whitelist state.
223	
224	Do not implement `AssetSale.sol` or `AssetFactory.sol` in this phase.
225	
226	---
227	
228	## Step 3: Implement Automated Unit Tests
229	
230	Create or update:
231	
232	`test/AssetToken.test.js`
233	
234	Use the testing framework already configured in Phase 1.
235	
236	Tests must be deterministic and must not require Sepolia, MetaMask, live network access, or real ETH.
237	
238	Use multiple local test accounts:
239	
240	```text
241	Account A: Issuer / Compliance Admin
242	Account B: Approved Investor 1
243	Account C: Approved Investor 2
244	Account D: Unapproved Investor
245	Account E: Unauthorised Administrator
246	```
247	
248	### Test Group A — Token Deployment
249	
250	Verify:
251	
252	1. Correct token name.
253	2. Correct token symbol.
254	3. Decimals equal 0.
255	4. Initial total supply equals 10,000.
256	5. Issuer initially receives 10,000 tokens.
257	6. Issuer is automatically whitelisted.
258	7. Issuer receives the required administrator roles.
259	8. Invalid issuer addresses are rejected.
260	9. Zero supply is rejected.
261	10. No externally accessible function can arbitrarily mint additional tokens.
262	
263	### Test Group B — Investor Whitelisting
264	
265	Verify:
266	
267	1. Compliance admin can whitelist Account B.
268	2. Compliance admin can whitelist Account C.
269	3. Approved addresses return `true` from the whitelist.
270	4. Compliance admin can revoke Account B.
271	5. Revoked addresses return `false`.
272	6. Unauthorised Account E cannot whitelist investors.
273	7. Unauthorised Account E cannot revoke investors.
274	8. Whitelist modifications emit the expected event.
275	9. Attempts to whitelist the zero address revert.
276	10. Revoking a wallet does not silently change its token balance.
277	
278	### Test Group C — ERC-20 Transfers
279	
280	Test the following sequence:
281	
282	1. Deploy CPT with 10,000 tokens.
283	2. Whitelist Account B.
284	3. Transfer 100 CPT from issuer to Account B.
285	4. Verify issuer balance equals 9,900.
286	5. Verify Account B balance equals 100.
287	6. Attempt transferring tokens from Account B to unapproved Account D.
288	7. Confirm the transaction reverts.
289	8. Verify all token balances remain unchanged after the revert.
290	9. Whitelist Account C.
291	10. Transfer 20 CPT from Account B to Account C.
292	11. Verify Account B now holds 80 CPT.
293	12. Verify Account C now holds 20 CPT.
294	13. Revoke Account B's whitelist status.
295	14. Verify Account B can neither send nor receive tokens.
296	15. Reapprove Account B.
297	16. Confirm transfers become possible again.
298	
299	### Test Group D — Delegated Transfers
300	
301	Test `approve()` and `transferFrom()`.
302	
303	Verify:
304	
305	- Allowances are created correctly.
306	- An approved delegated transfer between whitelisted holders succeeds.
307	- Delegated transfers to non-whitelisted recipients revert.
308	- Delegated transfers from non-whitelisted token holders revert.
309	- Failed delegated transfers do not unexpectedly alter balances or allowances.
310	- Standard ERC-20 insufficient-allowance behaviour is preserved.
311	
312	Be careful not to confuse the spender with the actual token sender. Compliance checks must cover the token holder (`from`) and recipient (`to`).
313	
314	### Test Group E — Edge Cases
315	
316	Include tests for:
317	
318	- Transfers exceeding the sender's balance.
319	- Transfers of zero tokens.
320	- Transfers to the zero address.
321	- Repeated whitelist updates.
322	- Token balance invariants.
323	- Revocation and subsequent reapproval.
324	- Independent whitelist states across two deployed asset-token instances.
325	- A token whose issuer differs from the deploying account, simulating deployment by a future factory.
326	
327	Use meaningful test descriptions so failures are understandable.
328	
329	---
330	
331	## Step 4: Validate the Implementation
332	
333	After implementation:
334	
335	1. Compile all Solidity contracts.
336	2. Run the complete Phase 2 test suite.
337	3. Run any existing repository tests to detect regressions.
338	4. Fix all compilation errors and failing tests.
339	5. Check for common Solidity security problems.
340	6. Remove unnecessary code and unused imports.
341	7. Ensure code style matches the existing project.
342	8. Verify compatibility with the installed OpenZeppelin version.
343	
344	Run the actual relevant build and test commands, rather than merely describing what should be run.
345	
346	If existing failures are unrelated to Phase 2, document them without making unrelated changes.
347	
348	Do not claim any test passed unless you executed it successfully.
349	
350	---
351	
352	## Step 5: Documentation and AI Audit Evidence
353	
354	The SC4053 assignment requires an AI Audit Report evaluating AI-assisted development.
355	
356	Maintain an accurate and reviewable record of this phase.
357

# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 2: Asset Tokenisation and Compliance

## Project Context

We are developing a decentralised application (dApp) titled **Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum** for the NTU SC4053 Blockchain Technology Development Project.

The application simulates an institutional real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation platform, inspired by financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC.

Users will eventually be able to create tokenised assets, purchase tokens using testnet ETH, manage investor permissions, and transfer tokens between eligible wallets.

The project is being developed in six sequential phases:

1. Project Foundation and Architecture — COMPLETED
2. Asset Tokenisation and Compliance — CURRENT PHASE
3. Asset Registry and Primary Issuance
4. Frontend and MetaMask Integration
5. End-to-End Integration and Testnet Deployment
6. Security Audit, AI Evaluation and Final Submission

**Your task is to fully implement Phase 2, including Solidity development, automated testing, validation, and technical documentation.**

Do not implement functionality belonging to later phases.

---

## Step 1: Inspect the Existing Repository

Before writing any code:

1. Read the existing README, project specifications, architecture documents, and relevant source files.
2. Inspect the Hardhat configuration, Solidity compiler version, OpenZeppelin version, package dependencies, and testing framework.
3. Understand the architecture established in Phase 1.
4. Identify any existing smart contracts or tests relevant to Phase 2.
5. Run the existing baseline tests, if available.
6. Preserve working Phase 1 code and established project conventions.

If there are minor differences between this prompt and the existing repository architecture, adapt the implementation to preserve compatibility. Document any meaningful architectural decisions.

Do not unnecessarily reinstall dependencies, overwrite configurations, introduce new frameworks, or restructure the project.

## Step 2: Implement `AssetToken.sol`

Create or complete:

`contracts/AssetToken.sol`

This is the core token contract representing fractional interests in a simulated real-world or digital asset.

### 2.1 ERC-20 Implementation

Use OpenZeppelin's ERC-20 implementation rather than writing token accounting from scratch.

The contract must support:

- Token name and symbol.
- Fixed initial token supply.
- Token balances.
- Standard `transfer`, `approve`, `allowance`, and `transferFrom` functionality.
- ERC-20 `Transfer` and `Approval` events.
- Ownership records derived from token balances.

The contract constructor should accept:

```solidity
constructor(
    string memory name_,
    string memory symbol_,
    uint256 initialSupply_,
    address issuer_
)
```

Expected behaviour:

- The token name and symbol are configured at deployment.
- `initialSupply_` is minted to the issuer's wallet.
- `totalSupply()` returns the correct fixed supply.
- `balanceOf(issuer_)` initially equals `initialSupply_`.
- Token decimals are set to **0**, representing whole asset units.
- Further minting is not permitted after deployment.
- Zero issuer addresses and zero initial supply must be rejected.

For example:

```text
Token Name: Campus Property Token
Symbol: CPT
Initial Supply: 10,000
Decimals: 0

Issuer Balance: 10,000 CPT
Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
```

The MVP uses whole token units. Do not automatically multiply the supply by 10^18.

### 2.2 Role-Based Access Control

Implement role-based permissions using OpenZeppelin AccessControl.

At minimum, define:

```solidity
bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE =
    keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE");
```

The issuer supplied during deployment should initially receive:

- `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`
- `COMPLIANCE_ROLE`

The issuer must also automatically be whitelisted.

Only authorised compliance administrators may approve or revoke investor eligibility.

Important implementation detail: **Do not assume `msg.sender` is always the issuer during construction.**

In Phase 3, the token contract may be deployed by an asset factory on behalf of an issuer. Therefore, roles must be explicitly assigned to the `issuer_` constructor argument rather than blindly assigned to the deploying contract.

Do not implement the platform-wide issuer approval system yet; that belongs to Phase 3.

### 2.3 Investor Whitelisting

Implement an on-chain investor eligibility registry.

Suggested state variable:

```solidity
mapping(address => bool) public isWhitelisted;
```

Required function:

```solidity
function setWhitelisted(
    address investor,
    bool approved
) external;
```

Requirements:

1. Only addresses holding `COMPLIANCE_ROLE` may call the function.
2. Setting `approved = true` adds an investor to the whitelist.
3. Setting `approved = false` revokes an investor's eligibility.
4. Zero addresses cannot be whitelisted.
5. Emit a `WhitelistUpdated` event when eligibility changes.
6. Whitelist status must be publicly readable.

An approved investor is permitted to hold and receive the asset tokens.

An investor removed from the whitelist must no longer be able to send or receive tokens, even if they still have a positive token balance.

Do not forcibly confiscate or burn tokens when whitelist access is revoked.

### 2.4 Enforce Transfer Restrictions

This is the most important functionality of Phase 2.

Modify ERC-20 transfer behaviour so that tokens can only move between whitelisted addresses.

Expected behaviour:

| Sender | Recipient | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer succeeds |
| Whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
| Not whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
| Not whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |

**The restrictions must be enforced inside the token contract itself, not just in a separate purchasing contract or frontend.**

Both `transfer()` and `transferFrom()` must respect the restrictions.

If OpenZeppelin Contracts v5 is installed, use the appropriate ERC-20 `_update()` override to enforce transfer eligibility. If an older compatible version is already used by the project, implement the equivalent restriction using the supported hook for that version.

Do not downgrade OpenZeppelin or use deprecated methods just to follow an example.

Handle the zero-address minting case correctly during initial deployment.

The initial mint must succeed even though the zero address is not an eligible investor.

Avoid adding unnecessary restrictions to standard ERC-20 approval functionality unless required for security.

### 2.5 Contract Events and Errors

Implement clear events for compliance operations, such as:

```solidity
event WhitelistUpdated(
    address indexed investor,
    bool approved,
    address indexed operator
);
```

Use descriptive custom errors where appropriate.

The code should clearly distinguish failures caused by:

- Unauthorised compliance administration.
- Invalid wallet addresses.
- Non-whitelisted senders.
- Non-whitelisted recipients.
- Invalid constructor parameters.

Keep the implementation concise and readable.

### 2.6 Future Compatibility

The contract must be designed to support Phase 3 without major redesign.

In Phase 3, an `AssetSale` contract will temporarily hold token inventory and distribute tokens to approved investors.

Therefore:

- Compliance administrators must be able to whitelist smart-contract addresses, not only externally owned wallets.
- Whitelisted sale contracts must be capable of receiving and transferring asset tokens.
- The token should work when instantiated by a factory contract.
- The token must not depend on any frontend implementation.
- Each deployed token must maintain independent balances, roles, and whitelist state.

Do not implement `AssetSale.sol` or `AssetFactory.sol` in this phase.

---

## Step 3: Implement Automated Unit Tests

Create or update:

`test/AssetToken.test.js`

Use the testing framework already configured in Phase 1.

Tests must be deterministic and must not require Sepolia, MetaMask, live network access, or real ETH.

Use multiple local test accounts:

```text
Account A: Issuer / Compliance Admin
Account B: Approved Investor 1
Account C: Approved Investor 2
Account D: Unapproved Investor
Account E: Unauthorised Administrator
```

### Test Group A — Token Deployment

Verify:

1. Correct token name.
2. Correct token symbol.
3. Decimals equal 0.
4. Initial total supply equals 10,000.
5. Issuer initially receives 10,000 tokens.
6. Issuer is automatically whitelisted.
7. Issuer receives the required administrator roles.
8. Invalid issuer addresses are rejected.
9. Zero supply is rejected.
10. No externally accessible function can arbitrarily mint additional tokens.

### Test Group B — Investor Whitelisting

Verify:

1. Compliance admin can whitelist Account B.
2. Compliance admin can whitelist Account C.
3. Approved addresses return `true` from the whitelist.
4. Compliance admin can revoke Account B.
5. Revoked addresses return `false`.
6. Unauthorised Account E cannot whitelist investors.
7. Unauthorised Account E cannot revoke investors.
8. Whitelist modifications emit the expected event.
9. Attempts to whitelist the zero address revert.
10. Revoking a wallet does not silently change its token balance.

### Test Group C — ERC-20 Transfers

Test the following sequence:

1. Deploy CPT with 10,000 tokens.
2. Whitelist Account B.
3. Transfer 100 CPT from issuer to Account B.
4. Verify issuer balance equals 9,900.
5. Verify Account B balance equals 100.
6. Attempt transferring tokens from Account B to unapproved Account D.
7. Confirm the transaction reverts.
8. Verify all token balances remain unchanged after the revert.
9. Whitelist Account C.
10. Transfer 20 CPT from Account B to Account C.
11. Verify Account B now holds 80 CPT.
12. Verify Account C now holds 20 CPT.
13. Revoke Account B's whitelist status.
14. Verify Account B can neither send nor receive tokens.
15. Reapprove Account B.
16. Confirm transfers become possible again.

### Test Group D — Delegated Transfers

Test `approve()` and `transferFrom()`.

Verify:

- Allowances are created correctly.
- An approved delegated transfer between whitelisted holders succeeds.
- Delegated transfers to non-whitelisted recipients revert.
- Delegated transfers from non-whitelisted token holders revert.
- Failed delegated transfers do not unexpectedly alter balances or allowances.
- Standard ERC-20 insufficient-allowance behaviour is preserved.

Be careful not to confuse the spender with the actual token sender. Compliance checks must cover the token holder (`from`) and recipient (`to`).

### Test Group E — Edge Cases

Include tests for:

- Transfers exceeding the sender's balance.
- Transfers of zero tokens.
- Transfers to the zero address.
- Repeated whitelist updates.
- Token balance invariants.
- Revocation and subsequent reapproval.
- Independent whitelist states across two deployed asset-token instances.
- A token whose issuer differs from the deploying account, simulating deployment by a future factory.

Use meaningful test descriptions so failures are understandable.

---

## Step 4: Validate the Implementation

After implementation:

1. Compile all Solidity contracts.
2. Run the complete Phase 2 test suite.
3. Run any existing repository tests to detect regressions.
4. Fix all compilation errors and failing tests.
5. Check for common Solidity security problems.
6. Remove unnecessary code and unused imports.
7. Ensure code style matches the existing project.
8. Verify compatibility with the installed OpenZeppelin version.

Run the actual relevant build and test commands, rather than merely describing what should be run.

If existing failures are unrelated to Phase 2, document them without making unrelated changes.

Do not claim any test passed unless you executed it successfully.

---

## Step 5: Documentation and AI Audit Evidence

The SC4053 assignment requires an AI Audit Report evaluating AI-assisted development.

Maintain an accurate and reviewable record of this phase.

Create or update:

`docs/phase2-implementation.md`

Include:

- Smart-contract overview.
- Explanation of ERC-20 tokenisation.
- Constructor parameters.
- Access-control architecture.
- Whitelist mechanism.
- Transfer restriction logic.
- Relevant functions and events.
- Explanation of the OpenZeppelin implementation choices.
- How Phase 3 will integrate with this contract.
- Testing methodology and outcomes.

Also preserve evidence relevant to the AI Audit Report, using the existing documentation structure where possible.

Record:

1. The initial Phase 2 requirements.
2. How AI was used to generate or modify the implementation.
3. Major architectural decisions.
4. Any genuine bugs, security concerns or incorrect AI-generated code discovered.
5. Why each issue was problematic.
6. The actual fixes implemented.
7. Evidence demonstrating that the fixes work.

Do not fabricate vulnerabilities or pretend tests were performed.

If possible, preserve representative failing and passing tests for genuinely discovered issues.

---

## Step 6: Provide a Working Demonstration

Create a minimal local demonstration using automated tests or a Hardhat script.

The demonstration must prove the following:

```text
1. Deploy Campus Property Token
   Name: Campus Property Token
   Symbol: CPT
   Supply: 10,000

2. Verify:
   Issuer owns 10,000 CPT

3. Whitelist Investor B

4. Transfer 100 CPT:
   Issuer -> Investor B

5. Verify:
   Issuer: 9,900 CPT
   Investor B: 100 CPT

6. Attempt transfer:
   Investor B -> Unapproved Investor D
   Amount: 20 CPT

7. Expected:
   Transaction REVERTED

8. Whitelist Investor C

9. Transfer:
   Investor B -> Investor C
   Amount: 20 CPT

10. Verify final balances:
    Issuer: 9,900 CPT
    Investor B: 80 CPT
    Investor C: 20 CPT
    Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
```

This should run locally without requiring a connected wallet or deployed frontend.

---

## Step 7: Strict Scope Boundaries

This phase must implement only **asset tokenisation and compliance**.

Do not implement:

- Asset factory and asset registry.
- Primary token sale contracts.
- ETH payment functionality.
- Asset marketplaces.
- React frontend.
- MetaMask integration.
- Secondary-market trading.
- Price oracles.
- Dividend distribution.
- Token redemption.
- NFTs or ERC-721.
- Mainnet deployment.
- External KYC integrations.

Do not add unnecessary abstractions, upgradeable proxies, or complex external dependencies.

Focus on a clean, secure, well-tested implementation.

---

## Step 8: Final Acceptance Criteria

Phase 2 is complete only when:

- [ ] `AssetToken.sol` implements a working ERC-20 token.
- [ ] Tokens are minted correctly to the designated issuer.
- [ ] Total token supply is fixed.
- [ ] Token decimals are 0.
- [ ] Role-based administrative permissions work.
- [ ] Issuers/compliance administrators can whitelist investors.
- [ ] Unauthorised wallets cannot modify whitelist permissions.
- [ ] Only whitelisted wallets can send and receive tokens.
- [ ] Both `transfer` and `transferFrom` enforce restrictions.
- [ ] Revoked wallets cannot transfer tokens.
- [ ] Multiple independent token instances work.
- [ ] The full automated test suite passes.
- [ ] The demonstration scenario succeeds.
- [ ] Documentation is updated.
- [ ] AI-assisted development and any discovered issues are accurately documented.
- [ ] Existing Phase 1 functionality remains intact.

## Expected Final Response

Once implementation and testing are complete, provide a structured report containing:

**1. Files Created/Modified**
List every file changed and explain its purpose.

**2. Implementation Summary**
Explain what was built and the important contract-design decisions.

**3. Testing Results**
Provide the actual commands executed, number of tests passing/failing, and relevant terminal output.

**4. Security Considerations**
Describe access-control, whitelisting, transfer-restriction and supply-integrity protections.

**5. Issues Discovered**
Report any genuine errors encountered and how they were fixed.

**6. Phase 2 Completion Status**
State which acceptance criteria are satisfied and which, if any, remain incomplete.

**7. Phase 3 Readiness**
Explain how the finished `AssetToken` contract can integrate with the future asset factory and primary issuance contracts.

### Important Development Instructions

- Implement the functionality; do not stop after writing a plan.
- Inspect the repository before modifying files.
- Preserve Phase 1 architecture wherever possible.
- Prefer established OpenZeppelin implementations.
- Write and execute automated tests.

**Begin by inspecting the current repository, then complete Phase 2 from implementation through automated validation.**

## Task 3.1 — Implement AssetFactory.sol

The factory will act as the entry point for new asset issuance.

It should provide these functions:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `authorizeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin grants issuer permission |
| `revokeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin removes issuer creation permission |
| `createAsset(...)` | Authorised issuer creates an asset |
| `getAsset(assetId)` | Returns asset metadata and contract addresses |
| `getAssetCount()` | Returns number of registered assets |

A successful `createAsset()` should deploy an AssetToken and associated AssetSale, then record the asset in the registry.

Suggested metadata:

```text
assetId
name
symbol
description
assetType
totalSupply
tokenContract
saleContract
issuerAddress
unitPriceWei
```

The asset ID should be generated automatically rather than supplied by the issuer.

## Task 3.2 — Implement AssetSale.sol

This contract will facilitate primary-market purchases.

Essential variables:

```solidity
IERC20 public assetToken;
address public issuer;
uint256 public pricePerToken;
```

Main function:

```solidity
buyTokens(uint256 quantity) external payable
```

Purchase validation must confirm:

- The buyer is an approved investor.
- Quantity is greater than zero.
- Enough tokens remain in the sale contract.
- `msg.value` equals `quantity * pricePerToken`.

If every condition passes, the contract transfers tokens to the investor and records the purchase event.

Use exact payment for the MVP; partial payments, complex refunds and variable pricing are unnecessary.

## Task 3.3 — Implement the inventory funding process

The issuer must allocate tokens to the sale contract before buyers can purchase them.

The lifecycle will be:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Issuer creates an asset | 10,000 CPT minted to issuer |
| Issuer whitelists the sale contract | Contract is permitted to hold and transfer CPT |
| Issuer deposits 5,000 CPT for sale | Sale contract now has purchasable inventory |
| Investor buys 100 CPT | Investor pays 0.1 testnet ETH and receives 100 CPT |

To simplify the MVP, the price is fixed at asset creation. Later changes to the sale price are not supported.

## Task 3.4 — Implement issuer withdrawals

Create an issuer-only withdrawal function for sale proceeds.

The function must prevent unauthorised withdrawals and account for reentrancy risks when sending ETH. Include a protected way to recover any unsold token inventory if the sale is closed.

## Task 3.5 — Test factory and sale contracts

Test the following scenarios:

| Test case | Expected result |
|---|---|
| Unauthorised wallet creates an asset | Revert |
| Authorised issuer creates asset | Token and sale contracts deployed |
| Issuer creates two different assets | Both registered independently |
| Whitelisted investor buys 100 tokens | Correct ETH payment and token transfer |
| Investor underpays | Revert |
| Investor overpays | Revert |
| Investor buys more than inventory | Revert |
| Unapproved investor attempts purchase | Revert |
| Non-issuer withdraws proceeds | Revert |

Phase 3 completion criteria: From a Hardhat script or console, you should be able to register an issuer, create an asset, whitelist an investor, fund the sale contract, execute a purchase and inspect the updated balances.

You now have a working blockchain backend.

---

## Additional constraints from the session brief

- Implement AssetFactory and AssetSale only. Do not add pause, freeze or forced transfer to AssetToken in this phase; that needs a separate team decision.
- `withdrawProceeds` must follow checks-effects-interactions (spec-v1 §4 reentrancy requirement, invariant 8).
- `revokeIssuer` only blocks future `createAsset` calls. Contracts the issuer has already deployed keep operating (spec-v1 §5 note on `deauthoriseIssuer`).

## Decisions made by the user (23 October 2026)

Claude Code raised these conflicts between this request and `spec-v1.md` before writing code. The user chose:

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | spec-v1 and this request name functions and variables differently. Which governs? | **This request governs**, as Phase 2's requirements did. Use `authorizeIssuer`, `revokeIssuer`, `getAsset`, `getAssetCount`, `buyTokens`, `pricePerToken` and `assetToken`. spec-v1 names (`authoriseIssuer`, `deauthoriseIssuer`, `buy`, `priceWei`, `token`) are superseded. The test stub titles are updated to match. |
| D2 | What does `createAsset` take as metadata? | `createAsset(name, symbol, description, assetType, totalSupply, unitPriceWei)`. `assetType` is an enum: `AssetType { RealWorld, Digital }`. `assetId` is assigned automatically. |
| D3 | How is unsold inventory recovered? | An issuer-only, irreversible `closeSale()`. After closing, `buyTokens` and `allocate` revert, and an issuer-only `recoverUnsoldTokens()` returns the sale contract's entire token balance to the issuer. |
| D4 | The repo was mid-rebase of `fix/spec-corrections-phase1`. | Abort the rebase and merge the branch into `main` normally, so no published history is rewritten. |

# Spec v0: original proposal (pre-AI)

This is the team's proposal as written before any AI tool was used. It is the baseline for Report Section 1 (Initial Specification & System Scope).

Do not edit this file. It is tagged `spec-v0`. All changes go in `spec-v1.md`.

Date written: 23 October 2026
Written by: Chordia Laksh

---

Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum

The project would be inspired by the increasing adoption of asset tokenisation by major financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC. We aim to develop a simplified dApp demonstrating how traditionally managed assets can be represented, issued, transferred, and managed using blockchain-based tokens and smart contracts.

For our proposed MVP, we are considering the following features:

Asset tokenisation: An authorised issuer can create/tokenise an asset using an Ethereum token standard.
Investor wallet interaction: Users can connect their wallets and view their tokenised asset holdings.
Primary issuance and transfer: Users can acquire and transfer tokenised assets through smart contracts.
Ownership and transaction records: Asset ownership and transaction history are maintained transparently on-chain.
Issuer controls/compliance: Basic mechanisms such as whitelisting authorised investors or restricting transfers to approved addresses.
From a technical perspective, we plan to implement the system using Solidity smart contracts on Ethereum, together with a web-based frontend and wallet integration such as MetaMask. We would also explore relevant token standards and smart-contract mechanisms used for tokenised financial assets.

The broader problem we would like to explore is how blockchain can provide programmable ownership, transparent settlement, and more efficient transfer of assets, while also accounting for the permissioning and compliance requirements that distinguish institutional asset tokenisation from ordinary cryptocurrencies.
